title: The Owl and the Nightingale
description: A debate poem of 1,794 lines in octosyllabic couplets in which the Owl and the Nightingale dispute which of them is the more useful and virtuous bird, arguing before a judge (Master Nicholas of Guildford) on matters of song, morality, marriage, and the religious life. It is the masterpiece of early Middle English poetry, combining French courtly wit with native English proverb and invective.
plot_or_argument: The Nightingale accuses the Owl of ugliness and gloom, the Owl the Nightingale of frivolity and seduction; their quarrel ranges over theology, sex, and music, and both appeal to Master Nicholas of Guildford to render judgement — a judgement the poem never records.
narrative_structure: A continuous debate with prologue and framing judgment scene; the two birds' alternating speeches develop antithetical cases without resolution.
principal_characters: the Owl; the Nightingale; Master Nicholas of Guildford (named as judge)
meter_and_prosody: Octosyllabic couplets with enjambment and proverbial density; a sophisticated blend of French debate form and native English idiom.
historical_context: Probably composed in Dorset or the south-west around 1200 (the text names King Henry as dead, dating it after 1189); preserved in two manuscripts of the mid-thirteenth century (BL Cotton Caligula A.ix and Jesus College, Oxford, MS 29).
literary_significance: The outstanding literary achievement of early Middle English and the fountainhead of the English debate tradition that runs through Winner and Waster and the Parliament of Fowls to the seventeenth century.
attribution_notes: Anonymous, but the poem names Master Nicholas of Guildford as its hoped-for judge; the authorship_status reflects scholarly practice in referring the work to its internal speaker.
bibliographical_notes: BL Cotton MS Caligula A.ix; Jesus College, Oxford, MS 29. Standard edition: N. Cartlidge (2001).

title: Layamon's Brut
description: Layamon's verse chronicle of Britain, some 16,000 lines adapting Wace's Roman de Brut with additions from Welsh and English tradition, from the Trojan Brutus to the Saxon conquest, including the fullest early English account of King Arthur. It is the first major treatment of the Arthurian legend in English.
plot_or_argument: Following the Trojan Brutus's settlement of Britain, the poem recounts the line of British kings — Lear, Cymbeline, and above all Arthur, whose conquests, Round Table, and death it narrates at length — down to the Saxon victory and Arthur's prophesied return.
narrative_structure: A continuous regnal chronicle organized by successive kings, with Arthur as its structural and emotional centre.
principal_characters: Brutus; King Lear; Arthur; Guinevere; Merlin; Vortigern; Hengest; Cadwalader
meter_and_prosody: A hybrid line blending the native alliterative half-line with loose rhyme and French-derived couplets; formulaic and archaic diction.
historical_context: Composed by the priest Layamon of Areley Kings, Worcestershire, c. 1190–1215, in the generation after the loss of Normandy, when English was re-emerging as a literary language; preserved in BL Cotton MS Caligula A.ix (earlier, longer) and Cotton MS Otho C.xiii (later, shortened, fire-damaged).
literary_significance: The first Arthurian epic in English and the bridge from the alliterative tradition to Middle English romance; its Arthur material influenced the entire subsequent Arthurian tradition in England.
attribution_notes: Authorship secured by the prologue's self-naming of Layamon, priest of Ernleye (Areley Kings).
bibliographical_notes: BL Cotton MSS Caligula A.ix and Otho C.xiii. Standard edition: Barron and Weinberg (1995).

title: The Ormulum
description: A vast collection of verse homilies on the gospels read in the mass throughout the year, composed by the Augustinian canon Orm c. 1180, of which about a fifth survives (some 10,000 short lines). Its unique, meticulously consistent spelling system makes it a document of the first importance for the history of English.
plot_or_argument: Each homily paraphrases the day's gospel text and expounds it allegorically and morally, with explanations of names and doctrine for the instruction of the English laity.
narrative_structure: A sequential homiliary following the liturgical year, with each sermon divided between gospel paraphrase, allegorical exposition, and moral application.
principal_characters: Christ; the evangelists' figures (none dramatically developed)
meter_and_prosody: An unrhymed fifteen-syllable septenarius in short couplet lines, strictly syllabic; the spelling system (double consonants after short vowels) is unique and systematic.
historical_context: Composed c. 1180 by Orm, an Augustinian canon, probably of Elsham Priory, Lincolnshire, for his brother Walter; preserved in a single authorial or near-authorial manuscript, Oxford, Bodleian Library, MS Junius 1.
literary_significance: The most ambitious vernacular religious work of the twelfth century and a uniquely valuable witness to early Middle English phonology, orthography, and East Midland dialect.
attribution_notes: Named in the dedication: 'þiss boc iss nemmnedd Orrmulum forrþi þatt Orrm itt wrohhte'.
bibliographical_notes: Bodleian Library, MS Junius 1. Standard edition: R. Holt (1878).

title: Poema Morale
description: A sermon in verse of some 400 lines on the conduct of life and the last things, often called the earliest Middle English poem of any consequence: the aged speaker meditates on a misspent youth, the brevity of life, and the terrors and joys of judgement, urging repentance before death.
plot_or_argument: The speaker reviews the stages of life, the certainty of death and judgement, the pains of hell and the bliss of heaven, and counsels amendment of life while time remains.
narrative_structure: A monologic homily moving from personal confession through doctrinal exposition (death, judgement, heaven, hell) to exhortation.
principal_characters: the aged speaker
meter_and_prosody: The loose fourteener (septenarius) couplet of the earliest Middle English homiletic verse.
historical_context: Composed in the south of England c. 1170, in the Kentish or south-western dialect; preserved in seven manuscripts, the earliest in the Lambeth and Trinity homily collections of c. 1200.
literary_significance: A touchstone of early Middle English: its popularity (seven manuscripts) and its homiletic style anticipate the great penitential literature of the thirteenth century.
attribution_notes: Anonymous; the speaker's self-description as old is a homiletic persona.
bibliographical_notes: Lambeth Palace MS 487; Trinity College, Cambridge, MS B.14.52; and five other copies.

title: The Bestiary
description: A Middle English bestiary of 802 lines, probably of East Anglian origin, describing the nature of the lion, eagle, serpent, stag, whale, and other creatures and drawing from each a moral and allegorical lesson, in the tradition of the Physiologus. It is the earliest English bestiary to survive in the vernacular.
plot_or_argument: Each animal's natural history — the lion's sleep with open eyes, the whale luring sailors, the phoenix's rebirth — is expounded as a figure of Christ, the devil, or the Christian soul.
narrative_structure: A sequence of discrete animal exempla, each divided between natural description (natura) and moralization (significacio).
principal_characters: the animals (lion, eagle, serpent, stag, fox, spider, whale, siren, elephant, turtle-dove, panther, dove)
meter_and_prosody: Irregular rhyming couplets of varying length, with some alliterative ornament.
historical_context: Composed c. 1250, translated from the Latin Physiologus of Theobaldus; preserved uniquely in BL Arundel MS 292, with Norwich connections.
literary_significance: The link between the Old English Physiologus poems and the later English bestiary tradition, and a vivid example of medieval allegorical natural history in the vernacular.
attribution_notes: Anonymous.
bibliographical_notes: BL Arundel MS 292. Standard edition: in A Book of Middle English (Burrow and Turville-Petre).

title: Ancrene Wisse
description: A rule of life for three anchoresses, written in the West Midlands 'AB language' c. 1225–40: eight parts treating the devotional routine, the custody of the senses, temptation, confession, penance, love, and the inner life. It is the greatest prose work of early Middle English, celebrated for its psychological acuity, its homely and exact imagery, and its humane severity.
plot_or_argument: Addressing the anchoresses as a loving director, the author regulates their prayers and reading, anatomizes the temptations of the solitary life (with the famous allegory of the royal wooing of the soul), teaches the art of confession, and unfolds the degrees of love culminating in union with Christ.
narrative_structure: Eight books moving from outer rule (devotions, senses) to inner rule (heart, conscience) and love; interlaced with exemplary tales and allegories.
principal_characters: the three anchoresses (addressees); Christ as lover-king (allegorical)
literary_form: rule and devotional treatise in prose
meter_and_prosody: Rhythmical, alliterative prose of great art; concrete domestic metaphor (the anchorhold as house, the heart as its lady).
historical_context: Written in Herefordshire or the Welsh Marches for three sisters enclosed near a church, in the milieu that produced the Katherine Group; revised and translated into French and Latin, and copied into the sixteenth century.
literary_significance: The masterpiece of early Middle English prose and the supreme English contribution to the literature of the solitary life; its influence reaches the Cloud-author and beyond.
attribution_notes: Anonymous; authorship_status reflects scholarly consensus (the author is sometimes speculatively identified with a Dominican or Augustinian director).
bibliographical_notes: Corpus Christi College, Cambridge, MS 402 (authorial); BL Cotton MSS Nero A.xiv, Titus D.xviii, Cleopatra C.vi. Standard edition: B. Millett, EETS OS 325–326 (2005–06).

title: The Katherine Group
alternative_titles: The Lives of St Katherine, St Margaret, and St Juliana
description: Three prose lives of virgin martyrs — St Katherine of Alexandria, St Margaret of Antioch, and St Juliana of Nicomedia — written in the same West Midlands 'AB language' as Ancrene Wisse for a female religious audience. They are the classic Middle English saints' lives: rhetorically elaborate, vivid in their debates and torments, and fervent in their celebration of virginity.
plot_or_argument: Each saint refuses a pagan suitor and judge, defeats her learned or demonic adversaries in debate, endures spectacular torments, and wins a martyr's crown, with Christ or angels as her comforters.
narrative_structure: Conventional martyr-act structure (arraignment, debate, torture, death) enriched by long speeches and prayers; Juliana includes the saint's dialogue with a demon.
principal_characters: St Katherine; St Margaret; St Juliana; the tyrant-judges (Maxentius, Olibrius, Eleusius); the demons
meter_and_prosody: Rhythmical alliterative prose with the characteristic AB-language vocabulary and spelling.
historical_context: Composed c. 1190–1225 in the same Herefordshire milieu as Ancrene Wisse; preserved in Bodleian MS Bodley 34 and BL Royal MS 17 A.xxvii.
literary_significance: The founding texts of the AB language group and the model for Middle English hagiography in the thirteenth century and after.
attribution_notes: Anonymous; grouped with Ancrene Wisse and the Wooing Group by dialect and manuscript kinship.
bibliographical_notes: Bodleian Library, MS Bodley 34; BL Royal MS 17 A.xxvii. Standard editions: EETS OS 51, 248 (D'Ardenne; Millett and Reimer).

title: Hali Meiðhad
description: An alliterative prose epistle in praise of virginity, addressed to young women contemplating the religious life, in the AB language of the Katherine Group. It contrasts the blessedness of the virgin bride of Christ with the miseries of married life, in a rhetorical tradition going back to patristic treatises on virginity.
plot_or_argument: The author extols virginity as the highest estate, describes the joys of the heavenly bridegroom, and — in famously vivid passages — details the pains and humiliations of marriage and childbearing to urge his readers to choose the better part.
narrative_structure: A single sustained exhortation moving from praise of virginity through satiric anatomy of marriage to the rewards of the heavenly marriage.
principal_characters: the virgin reader (addressee); Christ as bridegroom
meter_and_prosody: Rhythmical, heavily alliterative prose of the AB language group.
historical_context: Composed in the early thirteenth-century West Midlands, in the circle of Ancrene Wisse; preserved in Bodleian MS Bodley 34 and BL Cotton MS Titus D.xviii.
literary_significance: The classic Middle English statement of the virginity ideal, and a prime exhibit of the period's energetic anti-matrimonial rhetoric (the counterpart of the Wife of Bath's prologue).
attribution_notes: Anonymous.
bibliographical_notes: Bodleian Library, MS Bodley 34; BL Cotton MS Titus D.xviii. Standard edition: B. Millett, EETS OS 284 (1982).

title: Sawles Warde
description: An allegorical homily in AB-language prose on the custody of the soul: the house of the body is governed by Wit and Will, guarded by the five senses, threatened by the devil, and comforted by the virtues and the joys of heaven. It adapts Hugh of St Victor's De Anima and is the earliest extended allegory of the inner life in English prose.
plot_or_argument: Wit (reason), with his wife Will, rules the soul's house; the messenger Fear of Death warns of the devil's assaults; the virtues — Prudence, Strength, Moderation, Righteousness — and the vision of the heavenly bliss fortify the household against temptation.
narrative_structure: A continuous allegorical narrative built on the house/castle metaphor, with set-piece descriptions of the pains of hell and the joys of heaven.
principal_characters: Wit; Will; Fear of Death; the Virtues; the Devil
meter_and_prosody: Rhythmical alliterative AB-language prose.
historical_context: Composed in the early thirteenth-century West Midlands, adapting Hugh of St Victor; preserved in Bodleian MS Bodley 34, BL Cotton MS Titus D.xviii, and Royal MS 17 A.xxvii.
literary_significance: A foundation stone of English allegory: its personified psychology anticipates the moralities (The Castle of Perseverance) and the dream allegories of the fourteenth century.
attribution_notes: Anonymous.
bibliographical_notes: Bodleian Library, MS Bodley 34; BL Cotton MS Titus D.xviii. Standard edition: R. M. Wilson (1938).

title: The Wooing of Our Lord
alternative_titles: On Wel Swuðe God Ureisun of God Almihti
description: A group of lyrical prose meditations on the love of Christ, in the AB language: the Wooing of Our Lord, On Ureisun of Ure Louerde, On Lofsong of Ure Louerde, and related prayers. Addressed to a female recluse, they figure Christ as a knightly wooer whose love and Passion the anchoress must return, in prose of extraordinary affective intensity.
plot_or_argument: The speaker addresses Christ as lover and spouse, meditating on his beauty, his suffering on the cross, and the soul's answering love, weaving prayer, praise, and erotic-spiritual longing into a single meditation.
narrative_structure: A sequence of meditative addresses, each moving from invocation through Passion meditation to petition.
principal_characters: Christ as wooer; the anchoress speaker
meter_and_prosody: Rhythmical, alliterative, incantatory prose with lyric repetitions and refrains.
historical_context: Composed in the early thirteenth-century West Midlands for a woman recluse, in the same milieu as Ancrene Wisse; preserved in BL Cotton MS Nero A.xiv and Titus D.xviii.
literary_significance: The earliest English expression of the bride-mysticism and Passion devotion that culminate in Rolle, Julian, and the lyrics; a landmark of affective prose.
attribution_notes: Anonymous.
bibliographical_notes: BL Cotton MSS Nero A.xiv, Titus D.xviii. Standard edition: W. Meredith Thompson, EETS OS 241 (1958).

title: The Proverbs of Alfred
alternative_titles: The Proverbs of Alfred of Wessex
description: A collection of proverbial wisdom in verse, cast as the sayings of King Alfred assembled 'at Seaford' before a gathered folk, on kingship, wealth, wisdom, women, and the conduct of life. It is the principal early Middle English example of the native gnomic tradition continuing under the name of the great West Saxon king.
plot_or_argument: Alfred, enthroned at Seaford, delivers counsel in a series of proverb-laden sections — on wisdom and wealth, on choosing a wife, on old age — punctuated by the poet's own commentary.
narrative_structure: A framing scene of the king's council enclosing discrete gnomic sections with connective commentary.
principal_characters: Alfred (speaker); the assembled folk
meter_and_prosody: Loose alliterative and rhyming couplets in the transitional early Middle English manner.
historical_context: Composed c. 1150–80, perhaps in Sussex, in the south; preserved in Jesus College, Oxford, MS 29 (c. 1275) with The Owl and the Nightingale, and fragmentarily elsewhere.
literary_significance: The chief witness to the survival of the Old English wisdom tradition into Middle English, and a favourite anthology text of the early period.
attribution_notes: The attribution to Alfred is traditional and pseudonymous; the poem is the product of the twelfth-century cult of the king.
bibliographical_notes: Jesus College, Oxford, MS 29. Standard edition: in A Book of Middle English (Burrow and Turville-Petre).

title: The Land of Cokaygne
description: A rollicking satire of some 190 lines on the fantasy land of Cokaygne, a paradise of food, sleep, and license reached by a week in a sow's belly, whose abbey of gluttonous monks is described with anti-monastic glee. It is the earliest English example of the European Cockaigne tradition and a masterpiece of clerical self-satire.
plot_or_argument: The poet describes the geography of Cokaygne — roast geese flying, rivers of oil and wine, the fountain of youth — and dwells lovingly on the abbey where the monks, fattened without labour, fly about at their pleasure with the abbess.
narrative_structure: A catalogue-description of the dream land, closing with the burlesque of the monastic abbey.
principal_characters: the monks of Cokaygne; the abbess
meter_and_prosody: Octosyllabic couplets of comic energy, in an Irish-influenced Middle English.
historical_context: Composed c. 1300, perhaps in Ireland (the sole manuscript is the Kildare miscellany, BL Harley MS 913, c. 1330), where the Cockaigne tradition flourished among the friars.
literary_significance: The first English Cockaigne poem and the liveliest anti-clerical satire before Langland; a favourite of modern anthologies for its comic invention.
attribution_notes: Anonymous.
bibliographical_notes: BL Harley MS 913. Standard edition: in A Book of Middle English (Burrow and Turville-Petre).

title: The Fox and the Wolf
description: The earliest English beast fable, a comic tale of some 300 lines in which the fox, trapped in a bucket down a well, persuades the gullible wolf that he is in paradise, and escapes by the wolf's folly. It inaugurates the English Reynardian tradition that runs to Caxton's Reynard the Fox.
plot_or_argument: The thirsty fox climbs into one well-bucket and is stranded; when the wolf asks what he does there, the fox claims the well is paradise, induces the wolf to descend in the other bucket, and is drawn up as the wolf goes down.
narrative_structure: A single comic episode built on the trickster's persuasive lie and the dupe's comeuppance.
principal_characters: the Fox; the Wolf
meter_and_prosody: Octosyllabic couplets with lively dialogue.
historical_context: Composed c. 1250–75, adapted from the French Roman de Renart; preserved in the late thirteenth-century Digby MS 86 (Bodleian Library).
literary_significance: The beginning of the English Reynard tradition and the earliest English fabliau-fable; an essential witness to the continental debts of early Middle English narrative.
attribution_notes: Anonymous.
bibliographical_notes: Bodleian Library, Digby MS 86.

title: Dame Sirith
alternative_titles: The Interlude of the Clerk and the Girl
description: The earliest English fabliau: a comic tale of 450 lines in which the clerk Wilekin, failing to seduce Margery, buys the services of the old bawd Dame Sirith, whose trick with a weeping dog convinces Margery to yield. The poem may have been designed for performance by one or two speakers.
plot_or_argument: The lovesick clerk Wilekin woos Margery without success; Dame Sirith, hired for a fee, persuades Margery that her weeping bitch is a transformed woman punished for refusing a clerk — and Margery consents rather than share that fate.
narrative_structure: A short fabliau of courtship, trickery, and capitulation, largely in dialogue, with explicit staging cues.
principal_characters: Wilekin the clerk; Margery; Dame Sirith
meter_and_prosody: Irregular rhyming couplets with dialogue assignable to speakers (semi-dramatic form).
historical_context: Composed c. 1275 in the East Midlands; preserved in Bodleian Library, Digby MS 86 (c. 1300).
literary_significance: The first English fabliau and a landmark in the history of English comedy and secular drama; the bawd-and-trickster plot anticipates Chaucer's fabliaux.
attribution_notes: Anonymous.
bibliographical_notes: Bodleian Library, Digby MS 86.

title: The South English Legendary
description: The earliest great collection of verse saints' lives in Middle English, compiled in the south-west (probably Gloucestershire) c. 1270–85: a cycle of some 300 poems following the church year, from St Michael through the apostles and martyrs to All Souls. Its rollicking couplets and marvel-filled narratives made it the most popular legendary in medieval England.
plot_or_argument: Each entry narrates a saint's life, martyrdom, or feast — with dragons, tortures, and miracles — and draws the moral for the hearers; the collection includes the famous account of St Brendan's voyage and lives of English saints such as Thomas Becket.
narrative_structure: A calendrical cycle of independent verse legends, ordered by the liturgical year, in a frame of prologue and epilogue.
principal_characters: the saints of the calendar (Thomas Becket, Brendan, Edmund, Cecilia, and many others)
meter_and_prosody: Septenary (fourteener) couplets, loose and lively, designed for public reading.
historical_context: Compiled in the 1270s–1280s in the diocese of Worcester or Hereford, for parish and household reading; copied and expanded in some sixty manuscripts into the fifteenth century.
literary_significance: The foundational text of popular English hagiography and a principal source for Mirk's Festial and the later legendary tradition.
attribution_notes: Anonymous; compilational authorship by one or more clerical redactors.
bibliographical_notes: Bodleian Library, MS Laud Misc. 108 (earliest); some sixty manuscripts in all. Standard edition: C. D'Evelyn and A. J. Mill, EETS OS 235, 236, 244 (1956–59).

title: The Harley Lyrics
description: A collection of some forty secular and religious lyrics preserved in the Ludlow scribe's anthology, BL Harley MS 2253 (c. 1340), the richest single manuscript of early Middle English lyric: love songs, laments, satires, and devotional poems in French, Latin, and English, including such masterpieces as 'Alysoun', 'Wynter wakeneth al my care', and 'Blow, northerne wynd'.
plot_or_argument: The poems range across the lyric repertoire: the lover's springtime longing and complaint, the satire of corrupt clergy and unjust lords, the meditation on death and the Passion, and the praise of the Virgin.
narrative_structure: An anthology, not a sequence: the manuscript's trilingual arrangement (with English poems often paired with their French and Latin analogues) supplies the order.
principal_characters: the lovers and speakers of the lyrics
meter_and_prosody: A remarkable variety: tail-rhyme stanzas, alliterative long lines, and French-derived stanza forms, often with refrains.
historical_context: Copied c. 1340 by a professional scribe working near Ludlow, Herefordshire, for a gentry household, from materials of the later thirteenth and early fourteenth centuries.
literary_significance: The indispensable witness to the early Middle English lyric tradition at its best, and the principal source of the poems that bridge early and Ricardian poetry.
attribution_notes: Anonymous; the poems are the work of many hands, assembled by the scribe.
bibliographical_notes: BL Harley MS 2253. Standard edition: G. L. Brook, The Harley Lyrics (1948); S. Fein (ed.), TEAMS (2014–15).

title: The Middle English Lyric
description: The corpus of short Middle English lyric poems, secular and religious, composed and copied between c. 1200 and 1500: spring songs, love complaints, carols, lullabies, Passion meditations, and Marian praises, preserved in manuscripts and early printed collections. The most widely practised and most elusive of medieval English genres.
plot_or_argument: The corpus's subjects are love and spring, mortality and judgement, the joys and sorrows of the Virgin, and the Passion; many poems are songs, with refrains and burdens, meant for performance.
narrative_structure: A corpus rather than a single work; individual lyrics are typically stanzaic, with refrain patterns.
principal_characters: the lovers, mourners, and devotees who speak the lyrics
meter_and_prosody: Every available stanza form, from the tail-rhyme romance stanza to carol form, rhyme royal, and the macaronic hymn.
historical_context: Preserved in preaching manuscripts, commonplace books (Harley 2253; the Vernon manuscript), and, at the end of the period, in the printed collections of Wynkyn de Worde and Richard Pynson; the carol flourishes in the fifteenth century.
literary_significance: The lyric is the most continuous English poetic tradition of the period, feeding the courtly song of the Ricardians, the carol, and the Tudor songbooks.
attribution_notes: Anonymous as a corpus; individual poems occasionally attributable (e.g., to Rolle's circle or to Lydgate).
bibliographical_notes: Standard collection: C. Brown and R. H. Robbins, The Index of Middle English Verse (1943); T. G. Duncan (ed.), Medieval English Lyrics (2005).

title: Middle English Religious Lyrics
description: The devotional strand of the Middle English lyric corpus: meditations on the Passion ('I syng of a myden', 'Lullay, myn lykyng'), laments of the Virgin at the cross (the planctus Mariae), prayers to Christ and the saints, and poems on death and judgement. These lyrics carry the affective piety of the period into verse of great formal variety and emotional power.
plot_or_argument: The poems stage the central scenes of late medieval devotion — the Annunciation, the Nativity, the Crucifixion as witnessed by Mary, the soul's dialogue with the crucified Christ, the memento mori — in first-person, lyric form.
narrative_structure: A corpus of independent lyrics; the characteristic movements are invocation, meditation, and petition.
principal_characters: Christ; the Virgin Mary; the soul (speaker)
meter_and_prosody: Carol form, tail-rhyme, rhyme royal, and macaronic verse, often with musical settings implied by burdens and refrains.
historical_context: The lyrics were copied into preaching and devotional manuscripts (the Vernon manuscript, Digby 102, Sloane 2593) and printed in early sixteenth-century carol collections; many served Franciscan and parochial devotion.
literary_significance: The most intimate record of late medieval English piety; together with the mystery plays, the religious lyrics are the principal vernacular vehicle of Passion and Marian devotion.
attribution_notes: Anonymous as a corpus; a few poems are attributed to known devotional writers.
bibliographical_notes: Standard collections: C. Brown (ed.), Religious Lyrics of the XIVth and XVth Centuries (1924, 1939); S. Gray (ed.), A Selection of Religious Lyrics (1975).

title: Cursor Mundi
description: A vast northern verse history of the world, some 24,000 lines, 'running' (cursor) through sacred history from Creation to Doomsday: Old Testament narrative, the life of Christ, the Virgin, the apostles, and the finding of the cross. The most comprehensive biblical paraphrase in Middle English, designed to rival secular romance in the affections of its audience.
plot_or_argument: The poem retells the Old and New Testament story in chronological sequence — Creation, the patriarchs, Christ's life and Passion, the early church — with moralizations and legends (including the harrowing of hell) woven into the biblical narrative.
narrative_structure: A seven-part chronicle following the ages of the world, with prologue and epilogue framing the narrative as a book for 'lewed' men.
principal_characters: Christ; the Virgin Mary; the patriarchs, apostles, and saints
meter_and_prosody: Octosyllabic couplets (with some septenary sections) in the northern dialect.
historical_context: Composed c. 1300 in the north of England (Durham or Yorkshire), in the tradition of the Historia Scholastica and vernacular biblical paraphrase; preserved in nine manuscripts, with a southern version made c. 1400.
literary_significance: The largest Middle English biblical poem and the principal popular scriptural compendium before the Wycliffite Bible; a major witness to lay biblical culture.
attribution_notes: Anonymous.
bibliographical_notes: Nine manuscripts, incl. BL Cotton MS Vespasian A.iii. Standard edition: R. Morris, EETS OS 57, 59, 62, 66, 68, 99, 101 (1874–93).

title: Handlyng Synne
description: Robert Mannyng of Brunne's English verse adaptation (begun 1303) of the Anglo-Norman Manuel des péchés of William of Wadington: a manual of penance in some 12,000 lines expounding the commandments, the deadly sins, the sacraments, and the art of confession, illustrated with scores of exemplary tales. It is the classic Middle English penitential handbook.
plot_or_argument: The poem moves systematically through the commandments and sins, each doctrine illustrated by cautionary exempla — the dancing carolers cursed by a priest, the usurer, the witch of Ely — and concludes with instruction on confession, contrition, and satisfaction.
narrative_structure: A didactic sequence organized by commandment, sin, and sacrament, with narrative exempla inset throughout.
principal_characters: the exemplary sinners and saints of the tales
meter_and_prosody: Octosyllabic couplets of plain, efficient didactic verse in the Lincolnshire dialect.
historical_context: Begun in 1303 by the Gilbertine canon Robert Mannyng at Sempringham Priory, Lincolnshire, translating Wadington's manual for an English lay audience; preserved in the Vernon and Bodleian Digby manuscripts among others.
literary_significance: The principal English treatment of penance between the thirteenth-century homilies and Chaucer's Parson's Tale (which draws on related material), and a treasury of the exemplum tradition.
attribution_notes: Attributed by the author's own preface to 'Robert of Brunne'.
bibliographical_notes: Bodleian Library, MS Bodley 415; BL Harley MS 1701. Standard edition: I. Sullens (1983).

title: Robert Mannyng's Chronicle
description: Robert Mannyng of Brunne's verse history of England from Noah and the Trojan Brutus to the death of Edward I (1307), completed in 1338: the first part translates Wace's Roman de Brut, the second Peter Langtoft's French chronicle. It is the principal vernacular chronicle in English verse between Layamon and the fifteenth century.
plot_or_argument: The poem narrates British and English history in sequence — Brutus, Arthur, the Saxon kings, the Norman Conquest, and the Plantagenet reigns — with particular fullness on the baronial wars of the thirteenth century.
narrative_structure: A two-part regnal chronicle (Brut section; Langtoft section) with patriotic and didactic digressions.
principal_characters: Arthur; the English kings from William I to Edward I; Simon de Montfort
meter_and_prosody: Octosyllabic couplets in the first part, six-line tail-rhyme stanzas in the second.
historical_context: Completed in 1338 by Mannyng, Gilbertine canon of Sempringham, at Sixhills, for the instruction of lay readers in English history; preserved in two manuscripts, BL Harley MS 1317 and Lambeth Palace MS 131.
literary_significance: The chief English verse chronicle of the fourteenth century and a key witness to the national, vernacular historical consciousness of the period.
attribution_notes: Securely attributed to Mannyng in the poem's own colophon.
bibliographical_notes: BL Harley MS 1317; Lambeth Palace MS 131. Standard edition: I. Sullens (1996).

title: The Ayenbite of Inwyt
description: The Kentish translation, completed in 1340 by Dan Michel of Northgate, monk of St Augustine's, Canterbury, of the Somme le Roi of Frère Lorens: a comprehensive prose manual of the vices, virtues, commandments, and the art of holy dying. Its title — 'remorse of conscience' — gives the work its penitential keynote.
plot_or_argument: The treatise anatomizes the deadly sins and their remedies, the Ten Commandments, the Lord's Prayer, the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and the preparation for death, in a systematic scheme of moral and catechetical instruction.
narrative_structure: A systematic doctrinal handbook following the structure of the French Somme le Roi, with illustrative exempla.
principal_characters: none (doctrinal treatise)
meter_and_prosody: Prose; a famously conservative Kentish dialect with heavy French-derived vocabulary.
historical_context: Completed in 1340 at St Augustine's Abbey, Canterbury, on the eve of the Black Death; preserved in a single autograph manuscript, BL Arundel MS 57.
literary_significance: The most extensive Kentish text in Middle English, invaluable to historical linguistics, and a principal document of lay catechesis in the age of the Somme le Roi tradition.
attribution_notes: The translator names himself in the colophon: Dan Michel of Northgate.
bibliographical_notes: BL Arundel MS 57. Standard edition: P. Gradon, EETS OS 23 (1965; rev. 1979).
